{{Short description|Theorem}}
In the mathematical theory of [[stochastic processes|random processes]], the '''Markov chain central limit theorem''' has a conclusion somewhat similar in form to that of the classic [[central limit theorem]] (CLT) of [[probability theory]], but the quantity in the role taken by the variance in the classic CLT has a more complicated definition. See also the general form of [[Bienaymé's identity]].

== Statement ==

Suppose that:

* the sequence <math display="inline"> X_1,X_2,X_3,\ldots </math> of [[random element]]s of some set is a [[Markov chain]] that has a [[Discrete-time Markov chain#Stationary distributions|stationary probability distribution]]; and
* the initial distribution of the process, i.e. the distribution of <math display="inline"> X_1</math>, is the stationary distribution, so that <math display="inline"> X_1,X_2,X_3,\ldots</math> are identically distributed. In the classic central limit theorem these random variables would be assumed to be [[independence (probability theory)|independent]], but here we have only the weaker assumption that the process has the [[Markov property]]; and
* <math display="inline"> g</math> is some ([[measurable function|measurable]]) [[real-valued function]] for which <math display="inline"> \operatorname{var}(g(X_1)) <+\infty.</math>
Now let<ref>On the Markov Chain Central Limit Theorem, Galin L. Jones, https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0409112.pdf</ref><ref>Markov Chain Monte Carlo Lecture Notes Charles J. Geyer https://www.stat.umn.edu/geyer/f05/8931/n1998.pdf page 9</ref><ref>Note that the equation for <math>\sigma^2</math> starts from [[Bienaymé's identity]] and then assumes that <math>\lim_{n\to \infty }\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{(n-k)}{n} \operatorname{cov}( g(X_1), g(X_{1+k})) \approx \lim_{n\to \infty }\sum_{k=1}^n \operatorname{cov}( g(X_1), g(X_{1+k})) \to \sum_{k=1}^\infty \operatorname{cov}( g(X_1), g(X_{1+k}))</math> which is the [[Cesàro summation]], see Greyer, Markov Chain Monte Carlo Lecture Notes https://www.stat.umn.edu/geyer/f05/8931/n1998.pdf page 9</ref>
: <math>
\begin{align}
\mu & = \operatorname E(g(X_1)), \\
\widehat\mu_n & = \frac 1 n \sum_{k=1}^n g(X_k)\\
\sigma^2 & := \lim_{n\to \infty} \operatorname{var}(\sqrt{n}\widehat\mu_n) = \lim_{n\to \infty} n \operatorname{var}(\widehat\mu_n) = \operatorname{var}(g(X_1)) + 2\sum_{k=1}^\infty \operatorname{cov}( g(X_1), g(X_{1+k})).
\end{align}
</math>
Then as <math display="inline"> n \to\infty,</math> we have<ref>Geyer, Charles&nbsp;J. (2011).   Introduction  to  Markov Chain Monte Carlo.  In ''Handbook of MarkovChain Monte Carlo''.  Edited by S. P. Brooks, A. E. Gelman, G. L. Jones, and X. L. Meng.  Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, FL, Section 1.8. http://www.mcmchandbook.net/HandbookChapter1.pdf</ref>
: <math>
\sqrt{n} (\hat{\mu}_n - \mu) \ \xrightarrow{\mathcal{D}} \ \text{Normal}(0, \sigma^2),
</math>
where the decorated arrow indicates [[Convergence of random variables#Convergence in distribution|convergence in distribution]].

== Monte Carlo Setting ==

The Markov chain central limit theorem can be guaranteed for functionals of general state space Markov chains under certain conditions. In particular, this can be done with a focus on Monte Carlo settings. An example of the application in a MCMC ([[Markov chain Monte Carlo|Markov Chain Monte Carlo]]) setting is the following:

Consider a simple [[hard spheres]] model on a grid. Suppose <math>X = \{1, \ldots, n_1\} \times \{1, \ldots, n_2 \} \subseteq Z^2</math>. A proper configuration on <math>X</math> consists of coloring each point either black or white in such a way that no two adjacent points are white. Let <math>\chi</math> denote the set of all proper configurations on <math>X</math>, <math>N_{\chi}(n_1, n_2)</math> be the total number of proper configurations and π be the uniform distribution on <math>\chi</math> so that each proper configuration is equally likely. Suppose our goal is to calculate the typical number of white points in a proper configuration; that is, if <math>W(x)</math> is the number of white points in <math>x \in \chi</math> then we want the value of

<math>E_{\pi}W=\sum_{x \in \chi}\frac{W(x)}{N_\chi\bigl(n_1,n_2\bigr)}</math>

If <math>n_1</math> and <math>n_2</math> are even moderately large then we will have to resort to an approximation to <math>E_{\pi}W</math> . Consider the following Markov chain on <math>\chi</math>. Fix <math>p \in (0, 1)</math> and set <math>X_1 = x_1</math> where <math>x_1 \in \chi</math> is an arbitrary proper configuration. Randomly choose a point <math>(x, y) \in X</math> and independently draw <math>U \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0, 1)</math>. If <math>u \le p</math> and all of the adjacent points are black then color <math>(x, y)</math> white leaving all other points alone. Otherwise, color <math>(x, y)</math> black and leave all other points alone. Call the resulting configuration <math>X_1</math>. Continuing in this fashion yields a Harris ergodic Markov chain <math>\{X_1 , X_2 , X_3 , \ldots\}</math> having <math>\pi</math> as its invariant distribution. It is now a simple matter to estimate <math>E_{\pi} W</math> with <math>\overline{w_n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} W(X_i)/n</math>. Also, since <math>\chi</math> is finite (albeit potentially large) it is well known that <math>X</math> will converge exponentially fast to <math>\pi</math> which implies that a CLT holds for <math>\overline{w_n}</math>.

== Implications ==
Not taking into account the additional terms in the variance which stem from correlations (e.g. serial correlations in markov chain monte carlo simulations) can result in the problem of [[pseudoreplication]] when computing e.g. the [[confidence interval]]s for the [[sample mean]].
